source.title: Fluent Alignment with Disfluent Judges: Post-training for Lower-resource Languages
source.authors: David Samuel; Lilja Ovrelid; Erik Velldal; Andrey Kutuzov

page_placements.theme: A generative policy ends up preferred over its own weaker supervisor (an LLM judge or time-limited humans)

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses weak-to-strong generalization as an analogy, but does not test fine-tuning a strong model on a weaker model’s labels or otherwise test the listed claim versions. Its own experiments use on-policy reinforcement learning with judge-provided rewards.
record.gate_note: The study’s results concern whether an LLM judge’s fluency limits the fluency of an RL-trained policy, a related but different setup from the claim’s weak-label fine-tuning and PGR. The adjacent judge-policy fluency results are recorded under versions ["none"]. The paper’s SFT translation comparisons and other fluency ablations do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: No strong student is fine-tuned on a weaker supervisor's labels, and no PGR or strong ceiling is measured. The study trains policies with on-policy RL on rewards from an LLM judge. Its 'policy beats judge' result is on fluency, a quality the reward does not target. The authors cite weak-to-strong generalization only as an analogy (Section 5).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that on-policy RL yields fluent aligned models for lower-resource languages without target-language instruction data. In human evaluation it beats SFT on machine-translated data (67.5% head-to-head; 79.7% average win rate). Even small exposure to translated responses degrades fluency. Disfluent judges suffice if they understand the language. Weak-to-strong generalization is mentioned only as an analogy.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains policies with on-policy RL and judge-generated reward signals, rather than fine-tuning a strong student on a weaker supervisor’s labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The policy fluency scores vary little across the tested judges (92.1–94.2), while judge fluency ranges from 39.0 to 84.2; the authors report no apparent correspondence between judge fluency and policy fluency.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 8 judges, judge fluency ranges 39.0–84.2 while RL-trained policy fluency stays 92.1–94.2. The authors report Pearson r = 0.067 between the two.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On-policy RL with LLM-judge rewards yields policies more fluent than the judge, largely independent of judge fluency, when the policy was pretrained on the target language.

fits_no_version.finding: Native speakers prefer the on-policy RL model over its judge, Mistral Nemo, in 91.8% of pairwise fluency comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An RL-trained Norwegian policy is judged by humans more fluent than the judge model that supplied its rewards.

record.problems: The adjacent fluency results do not test weak-label fine-tuning or PGR. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the fluency scores or pairwise win rates; the main human comparison uses five raters and 100 prompts.
record.rows_left_out: Other fluency findings, including the training-length curves and SFT/translation-model ablations in Sections 4.3–4.5 and Tables 3–4, are not included because they do not test weak-supervisor label fine-tuning or another listed claim version.

untested.parts: No weak-label fine-tuning or PGR. The policy-vs-judge fluency gap uses RL rewards on overall quality, not the judge's labels on fluency.
No training change is compared on PGR.
No PGR by supervisor or student size or by task. The judge-size variation in Table 2 is on fluency under RL, not weak-label fine-tuning.
No exploitation, distribution-shift or shared-error tests.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'discusses'/T6 classification and versions ['none'] on all rows are correct. The judge is not a weak supervisor in the claim's sense. It scores overall response quality rather than providing labels, and the policy's fluency comes from target-language pretraining rather than from generalizing beyond weak labels.

versions.untested_parts: No strong student is fine-tuned on labels from a weaker supervisor; no weak-to-strong score or PGR is measured.
No training changes to weak-label fine-tuning are compared for PGR.
No PGR comparisons by supervisor or student size, task, or representation are made.
No weak-label student exploitation, distribution-shift PGR, or shared-error effect is tested.
No theoretical conditions for a student to outperform a supervisor are studied.

relation.reason: Section 5 discusses Burns and Charikar as related work and draws an analogy; the experiments do not test strong-student fine-tuning on weak-supervisor labels.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure preservation of pretrained Norwegian fluency during on-policy RL using judge rewards, not any listed weak-to-strong claim version. Fluency is not explicitly targeted by the reward.

source_check.notes: Observed states describe adjacent fluency results; no claim version is linked. Table 1 uses annotator-consensus wins with half credit for ties, so 91.8% is an aggregated win rate; Table 2 uses automatic sigmoid-normalized fluency scores.
